claim: ISG15 is an interferon-stimulated, linear di-ubiquitin-like protein, with anti-viral activity.
source: ISG15 is an interferon-stimulated, linear di-ubiquitin-like protein, with anti-viral activity.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ISG15's properties and function.

claim: ISG15 expression in nonphagocytic cells is dramatically induced upon Listeria infection.
source: We show that ISG15 expression in nonphagocytic cells is dramatically induced upon Listeria infection.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing ISG15 induction in nonphagocytic cells during Listeria infection.

claim: ISG15 induction by Listeria can be type I interferon independent.
source: Surprisingly this induction can be type I interferon independent and depends on the cytosolic surveillance pathway, which senses bacterial DNA and signals through STING, TBK1, IRF3 and IRF7.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data using B18R treatment and IFNAR2-/- cells showing ISG15 induction without type I interferon signaling.

claim: ISG15 induction by Listeria depends on the cytosolic surveillance pathway, which senses bacterial DNA and signals through STING, TBK1, IRF3 and IRF7.
source: Surprisingly this induction can be type I interferon independent and depends on the cytosolic surveillance pathway, which senses bacterial DNA and signals through STING, TBK1, IRF3 and IRF7.
evidence: The manuscript presents siRNA knockdown data and DNA transfection experiments supporting this pathway.

claim: ISG15 expression restricts Listeria infection in vitro.
source: Most importantly, we observed that ISG15 expression restricts Listeria infection in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from ISG15 overexpression, knockdown, and knockout cells showing reduced bacterial load with ISG15 expression.

claim: ISG15 expression restricts Listeria infection in vivo.
source: Most importantly, we observed that ISG15 expression restricts Listeria infection in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from Isg15-/- mice showing increased bacterial burden in liver and spleen.

claim: Infection or overexpression of ISG15 leads to ISGylation of ER and Golgi proteins.
source: Strikingly, infection or overexpression of ISG15 leads to ISGylation of ER and Golgi proteins, which correlates with increased secretion of cytokines known to counteract infection.
evidence: The manuscript presents SILAC-MS/MS data identifying ISGylated ER and Golgi proteins.

claim: ISGylation of ER and Golgi proteins correlates with increased secretion of cytokines known to counteract infection.
source: Strikingly, infection or overexpression of ISG15 leads to ISGylation of ER and Golgi proteins, which correlates with increased secretion of cytokines known to counteract infection.
evidence: The manuscript presents ELISA data showing increased IL-6 and IL-8 secretion in ISG15-overexpressing cells.

claim: Listeria monocytogenes is a food-borne pathogen that can cause enteric infections.
source: Listeria monocytogenes is a food-borne pathogen that can cause enteric infections.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Listeria monocytogenes.

claim: In immunocompromised individuals Listeria can cross the blood–brain barrier.
source: In addition, in immunocompromised individuals it can cross the blood–brain barrier and in pregnant women the feto-placental barrier potentially leading to cases of meningitis and septicemia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Listeria pathogenesis.

claim: In pregnant women Listeria can cross the feto-placental barrier potentially leading to cases of meningitis and septicemia.
source: In addition, in immunocompromised individuals it can cross the blood–brain barrier and in pregnant women the feto-placental barrier potentially leading to cases of meningitis and septicemia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Listeria pathogenesis.

claim: To be fully virulent, Listeria must evade macrophage killing, enter and replicate in epithelial cells and spread from cell to cell.
source: To be fully virulent, Listeria must evade macrophage killing, enter and replicate in epithelial cells and spread from cell to cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Listeria virulence mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: Listeria subverts a number of normal host cell functions in order to promote its own replication and dissemination through a plethora of well-characterized virulence factors.
source: Towards these aims Listeria subverts a number of normal host cell functions in order to promote its own replication and dissemination through a plethora of well-characterized virulence factors (Cossart and Lebreton, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Listeria induces a rapid and sterilizing CD8+ T cell-mediated adaptive immune response.
source: Conversely, Listeria induces a rapid and sterilizing CD8+ T cell-mediated adaptive immune response that has been extensively characterized (Lara-Tejero and Pamer, 2004; Pamer, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Listeria is able to survive and replicate in the cytosol.
source: Since Listeria is able to survive and replicate in the cytosol, several groups have sought to elucidate how bacteria are sensed within macrophages and more recently within nonphagocytic cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Listeria's intracellular lifestyle.

claim: Once Listeria has escaped from the phagosome, its multidrug efflux pumps secrete small molecules leading to activation of an IRF3-dependent cytosolic surveillance pathway, resulting in type I interferon activation.
source: Once Listeria has escaped from the phagosome, its multidrug efflux pumps secrete small molecules leading to activation of an IRF3-dependent cytosolic surveillance pathway (CSP), resulting in type I interferon activation (Crimmins et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cyclic-di-AMP is sufficient to activate interferon β production in macrophages.
source: One of these small molecules, cyclic-di-AMP, is sufficient to activate interferon β production in macrophages (Woodward et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In nonphagocytic cells, type I interferon induction seems to emanate from sensing of triphosphorylated RNA molecules via a RIG-I and MAVS-dependent pathway.
source: In nonphagocytic cells, type I interferon induction seems to emanate from sensing of triphosphorylated RNA molecules via a RIG-I and MAVS-dependent pathway (Abdullah et al., 2012; Hagmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Listeria activates the type III interferon pathway.
source: We have recently shown that Listeria also activates the type III interferon pathway (Lebreton et al., 2011; Bierne et al., 2012), a pathway which was discovered much later than type I interferon (Kotenko et al., 2003; Sheppard et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The type III interferon receptor has a more limited tissue expression pattern than the receptor for type I interferon but activates a signaling pathway similar to that of the type I interferon receptor.
source: The type III interferon receptor has a more limited tissue expression pattern than the receptor for type I interferon but activates a signaling pathway similar to that of the type I interferon receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type III interferon signaling.

claim: The type III response occurs via peroxisomal MAVS.
source: Strikingly, the type III response occurs via peroxisomal MAVS (Dixit et al., 2010; Odendall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISG15 is a linear di-ubiquitin-like molecule (ubl) that is conserved from zebrafish to human.
source: ISG15 is a linear di-ubiquitin-like molecule (ubl) that is conserved from zebrafish to human; however, it is much less well characterized than other ubls (Bogunovic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ISG15 can conjugate to over 300 cellular proteins.
source: It can conjugate to over 300 cellular proteins and can also function as a cytokine to induce interferon-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (D'Cunha et al., 1996; Giannakopoulos et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISG15 can function as a cytokine to induce interferon-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
source: It can conjugate to over 300 cellular proteins and can also function as a cytokine to induce interferon-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (D'Cunha et al., 1996; Giannakopoulos et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISG15 plays an important role in the innate immune response to viruses.
source: ISG15 plays an important role in the innate immune response to viruses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISG15 function.

claim: Isg15 expression becomes rapidly upregulated following type I interferon induction.
source: Isg15 expression becomes rapidly upregulated, and the protein is subsequently conjugated to cellular and/or viral targets following type I interferon induction (Zhang and Zhang, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ISG15 is conjugated to cellular and/or viral targets following type I interferon induction.
source: Isg15 expression becomes rapidly upregulated, and the protein is subsequently conjugated to cellular and/or viral targets following type I interferon induction (Zhang and Zhang, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mice deficient in ISG15 are susceptible to infection with Influenza, Sindbis, and Herpes viruses.
source: Mice deficient in ISG15 are susceptible to infection with Influenza, Sindbis, and Herpes viruses (D'Cunha et al., 1996; Lenschow et al., 2005, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many viruses encode proteins that specifically impair ISGylation.
source: Furthermore, many viruses encode proteins that specifically impair ISGylation (Frias-Staheli et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ISG15 can both modify specific target proteins and non-specifically modify proteins cotranslationally.
source: ISG15 seems to be unique among ubls, as it can both modify specific target proteins and non-specifically modify proteins cotranslationally (Frias-Staheli et al., 2007; Durfee et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISG15 is strongly induced by type I interferon, which is produced during bacterial infection.
source: Since ISG15 is strongly induced by type I interferon, which is produced during bacterial infection, we aimed to decipher whether ISG15 is induced during Listeria infection and if so whether ISGylation acts as a means of host defense against invading bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISG15 induction.

claim: Upon L. monocytogenes infection, ISG15 was massively induced, whereas incubation with the related non-pathogenic bacterium, Listeria innocua, did not lead to an increase in ISG15 production.
source: Upon L. monocytogenes infection, ISG15 was massively induced, whereas incubation with the related non-pathogenic bacterium, Listeria innocua, did not lead to an increase in ISG15 production (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 1A showing differential ISG15 induction.

claim: ISG15 protein levels increased relatively rapidly; the unconjugated protein was already present at 6 hr post infection and accumulated steadily throughout the infection.
source: ISG15 protein levels increased relatively rapidly; the unconjugated protein was already present at 6 hr post infection and accumulated steadily throughout the infection (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents time course immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: After 72 hr of systemic sub-lethal Listeria infection in mice, there was a robust induction of ISG15 and ISGylated conjugates in infected liver tissue.
source: After 72 hr of systemic sub-lethal Listeria infection in mice, there was a robust induction of ISG15 and ISGylated conjugates in infected liver tissue, revealing that Listeria infection leads to ISG15 induction both in vitro and in vivo (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data from mouse liver tissue in Figure 1C.

claim: ISG15 and IFNB1 transcripts are concomitantly induced after 3 hr of infection with Listeria.
source: Interestingly, we found that the two transcripts are concomitantly induced after 3 hr of infection with Listeria (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript presents qRT-PCR data in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Bacteria-induced ISG15 production was not diminished by B18R pretreatment in stark contrast to the interferon-induced ISG15 signal, which was almost entirely abrogated by B18R pretreatment.
source: We observed that bacteria-induced ISG15 production was not diminished by B18R pretreatment in stark contrast to the interferon-induced ISG15 signal, which was almost entirely abrogated by B18R pretreatment (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 1F showing differential effects of B18R.

claim: In the U5A cells (defective for type I interferon binding and signaling), as in 2fTGH cells, there is still a robust ISG15 response to Listeria infection.
source: Strikingly in the U5A cells (defective for type I interferon binding and signaling), as in 2fTGH cells, there is still a robust ISG15 response to Listeria infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 1G comparing 2fTGH and U5A cells.

claim: 2fTGH cells are unresponsive to type III interferon.
source: However, 2fTGH cells are unresponsive to type III interferon (Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The ISG15 protein induction observed is independent of both type I and type III interferon signaling.
source: Therefore, the ISG15 protein induction that we observed is independent of both type I and type III interferon signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the B18R and U5A cell experiments combined with knowledge about 2fTGH cells.

claim: Incubation of cells with L. innocua, a non-pathogenic Listeria species which cannot invade cells, did not induce ISG15 induction, demonstrating that external pathogen recognition receptors were not involved.
source: Incubation of cells with L. innocua, a non-pathogenic Listeria species which cannot invade cells, did not induce ISG15 induction, demonstrating that external pathogen recognition receptors were not involved (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 2A and infers the conclusion about external receptors.

claim: L. innocua that expresses Internalin B (InlB) was unable to induce an ISG15 signal, suggesting that the pathogen recognition receptors that survey the phagosome are not sufficient for ISG15 induction.
source: This strain was also unable to induce an ISG15 signal, suggesting that the pathogen recognition receptors that survey the phagosome are not sufficient for ISG15 induction (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 2A and infers the conclusion about phagosomal receptors.

claim: The Δhly mutant was able to potently induce ISG15.
source: Strikingly, we found that the Δhly mutant was able to potently induce ISG15 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 2A.

claim: LLO is not necessary for ISG15 induction.
source: Thus, LLO is not necessary for ISG15 induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the Δhly mutant data.

claim: In several human epithelial cell lines the mutant that lacks LLO (Δhly) can still escape into the cytosol.
source: However, in several human epithelial cell lines the mutant that lacks LLO (Δhly) can still escape into the cytosol (Portnoy et al., 1988; Marquis et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Listeria expresses two phospholipases that can compensate for the lack of LLO in the Δhly mutant in order to free the bacterium from the phagosome in human epithelial cells.
source: Listeria expresses two phospholipases that can compensate for the lack of LLO in the Δhly mutant in order to free the bacterium from the phagosome in human epithelial cells (Marquis et al., 1995; Smith et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The triple mutant (lacking LLO, PLCA, and PLCB) is unable to escape the phagosome of human epithelial cells.
source: This mutant is unable to escape the phagosome of human epithelial cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single mutants (either in PLCA or LLO), which escape into the cytosol, induce a strong ISG15 signal relative to non-infected cells.
source: Single mutants (either in PLCA or LLO), which escape into the cytosol, induce a strong ISG15 signal relative to non-infected cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: The triple mutant that is confined to the phagosome does not induce ISG15.
source: In contrast, the triple mutant that is confined to the phagosome does not induce ISG15 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Only cytoplasmic bacteria induce ISG15.
source: We thus conclude that only cytoplasmic bacteria induce ISG15.
evidence: This is inferred from the data with various Listeria mutants.

claim: The ΔactA mutant is unable to spread from cell to cell and cannot escape autophagic recognition, degradation, and lysis.
source: This mutant is unable to spread from cell to cell and cannot escape autophagic recognition, degradation, and lysis (Gouin et al., 2005; Yoshikawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ISG15 signal was clearly dependent on IRF3, IRF7, STING, and TBK1, implicating the CSP.
source: Our data showed that the ISG15 signal was clearly dependent on IRF3, IRF7, STING, and TBK1, implicating the CSP.
evidence: The manuscript presents siRNA knockdown data in Figure 2C.

claim: Depleting STAT1, which is a critical mediator of type I and III interferon signaling did not abrogate the ISG15 signal.
source: In further support of an interferon-independent signal, depleting STAT1, which is a critical mediator of type I and III interferon signaling did not abrogate the ISG15 signal (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents siRNA knockdown data in Figure 2C.

claim: In non-immune cells interferon induction has been linked to sensing of triphosphorylated RNA by RIG-I.
source: In non-immune cells interferon induction has been linked to sensing of triphosphorylated RNA by RIG-I (Abdullah et al., 2012; Hagmann et al., 2013); however, in our experimental conditions, RIG-I did not seem to be required for the ISG15 signal.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, combined with the authors' experimental data.

claim: In our experimental conditions, RIG-I did not seem to be required for the ISG15 signal.
source: In non-immune cells interferon induction has been linked to sensing of triphosphorylated RNA by RIG-I (Abdullah et al., 2012; Hagmann et al., 2013); however, in our experimental conditions, RIG-I did not seem to be required for the ISG15 signal.
evidence: This is based on the siRNA screen data.

claim: Direct ISG15 induction occurs through a pathway similar to the CSP in macrophages.
source: Instead, it seems that direct ISG15 induction occurs through a pathway similar to the CSP in macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA screen results.

claim: Listeria cyclic di-AMP led to an increase in IFNB1 transcript levels.
source: As expected Listeria cyclic di-AMP led to an increase in IFNB1 transcript levels.
evidence: The manuscript presents qRT-PCR data in Figure 2D.

claim: Listeria genomic DNA was the only PAMP sufficient for an increase in ISG15 levels.
source: Listeria genomic DNA was the only PAMP sufficient for an increase in ISG15 levels (Figure 2E), whereas ISG15 levels following cytosolic exposure to cyclic-di-AMP did not increase (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: ISG15 levels following cytosolic exposure to cyclic-di-AMP did not increase.
source: Listeria genomic DNA was the only PAMP sufficient for an increase in ISG15 levels (Figure 2E), whereas ISG15 levels following cytosolic exposure to cyclic-di-AMP did not increase (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 2D.

claim: The CSP can directly induce ISG15 after sensing of bacterial DNA in the cytosol of cells in a pathway that requires STING, TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7.
source: Collectively, these data implicate that the CSP can directly induce ISG15 after sensing of bacterial DNA in the cytosol of cells in a pathway that requires STING, TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined siRNA and PAMP transfection data.

claim: Stable overexpression of ISG15 resulted in 50% fewer cytosolic bacteria as compared to control cells after 3 hr of infection.
source: For the same multiplicity of infection (MOI) after 3 hr of infection, stable overexpression of ISG15 resulted in 50% fewer cytosolic bacteria as compared to control cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents CFU data in Figure 3A.

claim: ISG15 does not impact bacterial invasion.
source: We then assessed bacterial uptake by differentiating between the bacteria that are inside the cell or those that remain on the surface (inside-out staining) and did not observe a difference between control and ISG15-overexpressing cells for invasion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents invasion assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 7 and 12 hr post infection, there were still 50% fewer bacteria in ISG15-overexpressing cells, and by 24 hr, the levels of bacteria had equalized between the two cell lines.
source: During a time course of infection in these cells at 7 and 12 hr, there were still 50% fewer bacteria, and by 24 hr, the levels of bacteria had equalized between the two cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents time course CFU data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ISG15 does not impact bacterial replication as an active bacterial clearance mechanism would.
source: This time course suggests that ISG15 does not impact bacterial replication as an active bacterial clearance mechanism would (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the time course data.

claim: Knocking down ISG15 during infection increased bacterial load by nearly twofold after 15 hr.
source: We then knocked down ISG15 during infection. This increased bacterial load by nearly twofold after 15 hr (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents CFU data in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a fivefold increase in bacterial load in Isg15−/− MEFs compared to wild-type MEFs for the same MOI.
source: We infected these cells with Listeria and we observed a fivefold increase in bacterial load in Isg15−/− MEFs compared to wild-type MEFs for the same MOI (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents CFU data in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Isg15−/− MEFs are not susceptible to other intracellular pathogens such as Shigella flexneri and Salmonella typhimurium.
source: Interestingly, Isg15−/− MEFs are not susceptible to other intracellular pathogens such as Shigella flexneri and Salmonella typhimurium, and in HeLa cells only Staphylococcus aureus is able to induce as much ISG15 as Listeria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents CFU and immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In HeLa cells only Staphylococcus aureus is able to induce as much ISG15 as Listeria.
source: Interestingly, Isg15−/− MEFs are not susceptible to other intracellular pathogens such as Shigella flexneri and Salmonella typhimurium, and in HeLa cells only Staphylococcus aureus is able to induce as much ISG15 as Listeria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S. flexneri and S. typhimurium induce very little ISG15.
source: Indeed, S. flexneri and S. typhimurium induce very little ISG15.
evidence: This is based on the immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ISG15-deficient mice exhibited a significant increase in bacterial load compared to wild-type animals in both the spleen and liver after 72 hr of systemic sub-lethal Listeria infection.
source: ISG15-deficient mice exhibited a significant increase in bacterial load compared to wild-type animals in both the spleen and liver after 72 hr of systemic sub-lethal Listeria infection (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The manuscript presents in vivo CFU data in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: UBE1L (E1), UBE2L6 (E2), HERC5 and TRIM25 (E3s) mRNA are all significantly upregulated following Listeria infection.
source: We found that UBE1L (E1), UBE2L6 (E2), HERC5 and TRIM25 (E3s) mRNA are all significantly upregulated following Listeria infection, as is the deconjugating enzyme USP18 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNASeq data in Figure 3G.

claim: The deconjugating enzyme USP18 is significantly upregulated following Listeria infection.
source: We found that UBE1L (E1), UBE2L6 (E2), HERC5 and TRIM25 (E3s) mRNA are all significantly upregulated following Listeria infection, as is the deconjugating enzyme USP18 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNASeq data in Figure 3G.

claim: TRIM25 displayed increased expression relative to loading control at 3 hr post infection.
source: Interestingly, TRIM25 already displayed increased expression relative to loading control at 3 hr post infection.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 3H.

claim: UBE2L6 was present in these cells at 3 hr post infection.
source: UBE2L6 was present in these cells at this time point as well.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 3H.

claim: Primary MEFs that lack UBE1L have a much higher bacterial burden following Listeria infection than wild-type MEFs at 4 hr post infection.
source: Primary MEFs that lack UBE1L, and thus can not form ISG15 conjugates, have a much higher bacterial burden following Listeria infection than wild-type MEFs at 4 hr post infection.
evidence: The manuscript presents CFU data in Figure 3I.

claim: This phenotype mirrors the bacterial burden of Isg15−/− MEFs, clearly indicating that ISG15's role in host defense against Listeria in vitro requires ISGylation.
source: This phenotype mirrors the bacterial burden of Isg15−/− MEFs, clearly indicating that ISG15's role in host defense against Listeria in vitro requires ISGylation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the Ube1L-/- and Isg15-/- MEF data.

claim: Thirty ISGylated proteins were identified as modified following overexpression of ISG15.
source: We identified thirty ISGylated proteins modified following overexpression of ISG15 (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—source data 1, depicted in blue).
evidence: The manuscript presents SILAC-MS/MS data in Figure 4.

claim: These proteins have not yet been reported to be targets of ISGylation.
source: Interestingly, these proteins have not yet been reported to be targets of ISGylation.
evidence: This is based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: Following interferon treatment, ISG15 modified twelve additional proteins distinct from those that were ISGylated after overexpression without treatment.
source: Following interferon treatment, ISG15 modified twelve additional proteins distinct from those that were ISGylated after overexpression without treatment (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—source data 1, depicted in red).
evidence: The manuscript presents SILAC-MS/MS data in Figure 4.

claim: Three of the proteins ISGylated following interferon treatment are known targets of ISGylation following interferon treatment in the aforementioned screens.
source: Three of these proteins are known targets of ISGylation following interferon treatment in the aforementioned screens.
evidence: This is based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: Nine proteins ISGylated following interferon treatment are novel substrates of ISGylation.
source: The other nine are novel substrates of ISGylation.
evidence: This is based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: Over 80% of ISG15-target proteins are integral membrane proteins.
source: To our surprise over 80% of ISG15-target proteins are integral membrane proteins (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene ontology analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: ISG15-target proteins are known to be primarily localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus and/or are critical for glycosylation, ER morphology and ER to Golgi trafficking.
source: Even more intriguingly they are known to be primarily localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus and/or are critical for glycosylation, ER morphology and ER to Golgi trafficking (e.g., the oligosaccharyl-transferase (OST) complex, RTN4, ATL3, SEC22B, ERGIC1, and ERGIC3; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis and known protein functions.

claim: MAGT1 is critical for T cell activation and patients with a deletion in the MAGT1 gene are susceptible to viral and certain bacterial infections.
source: MAGT1 is critical for T cell activation and patients with a deletion in the MAGT1 gene are susceptible to viral and certain bacterial infections (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MAGT1 is localized to the cell surface or to the ER where it interacts with the OST complex, which is critical for N-glycosylation.
source: The protein is localized to the cell surface or to the ER where it interacts with the OST complex, which is critical for N-glycosylation (Pfeffer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Multiple proteins from the OST complex were identified as targets of ISGylation.
source: Notably, we also identified multiple proteins from the OST complex as targets of ISGylation (Figure 4C, inset).
evidence: The manuscript presents SILAC-MS/MS data in Figure 4C.

claim: Two higher molecular weight ISG15-MAGT1 complexes appear that are absent in control cells.
source: Two higher molecular weight ISG15-MAGT1 complexes appear that are absent in control cells (Figure 5B, arrows).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a higher molecular weight MAGT1 complex that immunoprecipitates with ISG15 following infection.
source: To assess whether MAGT1 was ISGylated following infection, we immunoprecipitated ISG15 and could show that there is a higher molecular weight MAGT1 complex that immunoprecipitates with ISG15 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Non-conjugated MAGT1 was enriched following ISG15 immunoprecipitation.
source: Additionally, non-conjugated MAGT1 was enriched following ISG15 immunoprecipitation as well.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MAGT1 is induced by Listeria infection.
source: Of note, MAGT1 is also induced by Listeria infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RTN4 is a target of ISGylation following ISG15 overexpression.
source: A second target of ISGylation following ISG15 overexpression is Reticulon 4 (RTN4) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents SILAC-MS/MS data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: RTN4 helps to determine the morphology of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: It is known that RTN4 helps to determine the morphology of the endoplasmic reticulum (Voeltz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Endogenous RTN4 was modified by ISG15 as detected by an upshifted ladder of modified RTN4 that was also recognized by the ISG15 antibody.
source: We also validated that endogenous RTN4 was modified by ISG15 by immunoblot (Figure 5B), and we detected an upshifted ladder of modified RTN4 that was also recognized by the ISG15 antibody.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data in Figure 5B.

claim: The ladder of modified RTN4 most likely corresponds to either multiple ISGylations of RTN4 or concomitant modifications of RTN4 by ISG15 together with other modifiers as opposed to a single modification.
source: ISG15 is not known to make chains so the ladder most likely corresponds to either multiple ISGylations of RTN4 or concomitant modifications of RTN4 by ISG15 together with other modifiers as opposed to a single modification.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoblot pattern and knowledge about ISG15.

claim: Endogenous modification of RTN4 by ISG15 occurs following Listeria infection.
source: Here again we could validate the endogenous modification of RTN4 by ISG15 following Listeria infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) by detecting multiple distinct slower migrating bands of RTN4 and ISG15 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atlastin-3 was identified as an ISG15 target.
source: Interestingly, Atlastin-3, another protein that affects ER morphology was also identified as an ISG15 target.
evidence: This is based on the SILAC-MS/MS data.

claim: Atlastin-3 is an ER dynamin-like GTPase that can alter the morphology of both the ER and the Golgi apparatus.
source: Atlastin-3 is an ER dynamin-like GTPase that can alter the morphology of both the ER and the Golgi apparatus (Rismanchi et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.
